clips.text: The tree stays at the center. Find a position using the fixed screen view.
Position is described relative to a reference object.
Place the sample above the tree.
What is the reference object? A. The tree B. Your moving finger
Build your explanation.
The sample is above the tree.
Use the same map. Left and right follow the screen, even if a character turns.
A fixed reference view makes instructions clear.
Place the box to the left of the tree.
If the worker turns around, does the map’s left side change? A. Yes B. No
Build your explanation.
The box is to the left of the tree.
Route A is 6 model units long; route B is 9. Align the ruler’s zero with the start.
Model units describe the drawing, not real centimeters on your screen.
Align zero with START, then measure.
Which route is longer? A. Route A: 6 units B. Route B: 9 units
Build your explanation.
Route B is longer than route A.
Give a direction that names both the target position and the reference object.
Clear directions identify a position and reference.
Place the parcel between the tree and the station.
Which instruction is clearer? A. Put it there. B. Put the parcel between the tree and the station.
Build your explanation.
Put the parcel between the tree and the station.
Watch a cart relative to the fixed flag. One trial goes out and returns.
Compare positions over time, not only the first and last pictures.
Replay both journeys.
It ends where it started. Does that prove it never moved? A. Yes B. No. We must watch the journey.
Build your explanation.
The cart moved even when it returned to its starting position.
Watch three separate model motions: straight travel, rotation, and back-and-forth travel.
Real objects may combine motions; these clips isolate one pattern.
Play all three motion clips.
Which clip goes out and returns? A. Rotation B. Back and forth C. Straight travel
Build your explanation.
Back-and-forth motion changes direction and can return to the start.
Model record: cart A travels 20 units in 5 seconds; B travels 30 in 5 seconds.
For equal times, compare distance traveled.
Run both carts for the same model time.
Which has the greater average speed? A. A B. B C. They must be equal
Build your explanation.
Cart B travels farther in the same time, so its average speed is greater.
Both carts travel 20 units. A takes 4 seconds; B takes 6 seconds.
Compare each cart’s elapsed travel time, not who starts first.
Run both equal-distance trials.
Which has the greater average speed? A. A B. B
Build your explanation.
Cart A takes less time for the same distance, so its average speed is greater.
The worker is at the left. A push sends this box right; a pull brings it toward the worker.
A push or pull is a force acting on an object.
Try pushing and pulling.
Which action brings the box toward the worker? A. Push away B. Pull toward
Build your explanation.
A pull brings this box toward the worker.
The cart starts at rest. The target is to its right. Compare two opposite pushes.
The effect of a force depends on its direction and the object’s current motion.
Test both push directions.
Which push moves this resting cart toward the right target? A. Push right B. Push left
Build your explanation.
For this resting cart, a push to the right starts motion toward the target.
Same cart, surface, start, and push duration. Change only the push setting.
Limit conclusions to the tested conditions.
Compare the two push settings.
What does this model record support? A. The stronger push sent this cart farther under these conditions. B. A stronger push always sends every object farther.
Build your explanation.
Under the same model conditions, the stronger push sent this cart farther.
We want to compare push strengths. Keep the cart, surface, start, and push duration fixed.
Changing several conditions together makes the cause harder to identify.
Sort the conditions for this push-strength test.
Why should the surface stay the same? A. It could also affect the cart’s motion. B. Surfaces never matter.
Build your explanation.
I keep the cart and surface the same. I change the push strength.
Same cart and starting speed on two level tracks. Compare how far it travels before stopping.
Use the recorded outcome for these materials, not a universal rule for every surface and wheel.
Run both surface trials.
Which surface slowed this cart more in these trials? A. Rough test track B. Smooth test track
Build your explanation.
On these test tracks, the rough surface stopped this cart sooner.
A transport path should be easy to travel along; a stopping area should help slow this cart.
Friction can be useful for grip or braking and can also resist movement.
Compare travel and stopping surfaces.
Where could increased friction help this model task? A. The stopping area B. Nowhere; friction is always bad.
Build your explanation.
Friction can help slow a moving cart in a stopping area.
Observe separate model clips of motion changing. The labels describe the force effect in each clip.
Motion changes when forces are unbalanced; continued steady motion does not require a continuous net push.
Watch both changes in speed.
Which statement is supported? A. Forces can change motion. B. A moving object must always be pushed continuously.
Build your explanation.
A force can speed up, slow down, or change the direction of motion.
Use a turn model, then a braking model. Observe the direction change and stop.
A force can change direction even if speed stays the same.
Run both control clips.
Does changing direction count as changing motion? A. Yes B. No
Build your explanation.
Changing direction is a change in motion.
Route A is shorter and takes 4 model seconds. Route B is longer and takes 6. Both reach the receiving point.
Different routes may trade distance, time, and ease of control.
Test both possible routes.
Which route used less model travel time? A. Route A B. Route B
Build your explanation.
Both routes reach the station. Route A takes less model time.
Target zone: 18–22 model units. Choose a braking setting and inspect where the cart stops.
A successful delivery meets the stopping condition, not simply the greatest distance.
Test a setting that stops inside the target zone.
Why does the middle setting meet the brief? A. It stops at 20, within 18–22. B. It travels the farthest.
Build your explanation.
I chose the braking setting that stopped the cart inside the target zone.
The previous trial stopped at 28 and overshot an 18–22 target. Keep the cart and route fixed; adjust braking.
Use a failed trial as evidence for the next test.
Test an adjustment and compare with the overshoot.
Which change addresses this overshoot? A. Brake earlier, keeping other conditions the same. B. Change the cart, route, and braking all at once.
Build your explanation.
The first cart overshot. I changed the braking point and kept the other conditions the same.
Delivery brief: stop in the receiving zone, 18–22 units along the route. Two different model plans can meet this requirement.
More than one plan can work when each meets the stated conditions.
Choose and test a plan that meets the brief.
Which explanation uses evidence? A. My tested plan stopped inside the required zone. B. My favorite color proves the plan works.
Build your explanation.
I tested a delivery plan. The cart stopped inside the target zone. The record supports my choice.
